name: Humming exercises

lead: Humming exercises use a sustained tone with the lips closed, so the sound resonates in the head and throat and passes through the nose. People use it as a gentle warm-up before speaking or singing, aiming for a smoother, more resonant sound.

The closed-mouth position is described as a low-effort way to begin phonating. Voice-training circles use it widely as a warm-up. Little research addresses humming for appearance-related voice outcomes.

paras: People hum for a few minutes before speaking, presenting or singing, often sliding gently up and down in pitch and feeling the buzz around the lips and nose. It is usually paired with other warm-ups.
No specific risks are documented. Voice clinicians generally advise stopping any vocal practice that causes pain or hoarseness.

angle.text: Humming is used as a gentle warm-up to ease the voice into a smoother, more resonant sound before speaking or singing. It is popular in voice-training circles, with little research on appearance-related outcomes.

lead: Humming exercises are voice warm-ups in which a person makes a wordless tone with the mouth closed, so the sound resonates in the nose, head and throat.[1] In voice-improvement discussions, people use them to ease into speaking or singing, loosen the voice before a conversation, call or performance, and get a smoother, more comfortable-sounding voice, which contributes to how they come across.

A hum is described as a monotone or lightly varying tone made with closed lips, and humming is also a feature of music, with melodies sometimes hummed rather than sung.[1] Vocal warm-ups in general are described as preparing the body, breath, articulators and resonators and moving from the speaking voice toward a wider range; nasal-sound exercises are used to direct sound toward the soft palate.[2]

Claimed benefits of warm-ups include reducing the sense of effort in singing and relaxing the neck and shoulders so that tension does not constrict the larynx.[2] A 2022 study cited by Wikipedia found that warm-up exercises temporarily increase self-assessed vocal effort, which returns to normal after a short rest.[2] No studies were found testing humming for changing perceived vocal attractiveness.
infobox: Nasal-sound exercises, lip trills, straw phonation

paras: Humming is described as a monotone or lightly varying tone made with closed lips, with air resonating in the passages of the head and throat.[1] It is also a feature of music, with melodies sometimes hummed rather than sung.[1]

Wikipedia's article on vocal warm-ups lists five goals: warming up the body, preparing the breath, preparing the articulators and resonators, moving from the speaking voice to a singing or projecting voice, and rehearsing the specific material. Resonance work includes directing sound toward the soft palate with nasal sounds.[2]
Claimed benefits include reduced effort, relaxation of the neck, shoulders and abdomen, and better breath control and diction. The article notes many of its claims are not directly sourced.[2]

Humming is mentioned in voice-improvement discussions as a warm-up alongside other vocal exercises. Related semi-occluded exercises, such as phonating through a straw, have a larger published literature in voice science.
